# fshy: Databases and KV in full

> Hosted databases, vector stores and key-value stores.

Data as of 2026-11-20, the date of the published data. Version `7e4259089a05`: the first 12 hex digits of the SHA-256 of every record's Markdown, topic by topic in the one order (hosted before self-hosted, then verdict, provider name, record id); it changes whenever a record does.

How to read a record, and the other topics: https://fshy.ajam.dev/llms-full.txt. One line per record: https://fshy.ajam.dev/t/databases-kv.md.

## Cloud Firestore (firestore)

- `databases-kv/firestore` | qualifies | evidence documented | binding request-rate | category document database
- needs card no, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-11-18T11:59:33.150Z (live) | stale on 2026-12-19
- url https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore/quotas | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/google.md
- free tier: 1 GiB stored, 50,000 document reads per day, 20,000 writes per day, 20,000 deletes per day, exactly one free database per project | unit: GiB | metered on: request-count | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 1 GiB stored; a 1 MiB document size limit applies to the engine | source: [1]
- retention: the free tier blocks, it does not delete: on the Spark plan a product whose no-cost quota is exceeded is shut off for the rest of the month, and it comes back at the next billing cycle or on an upgrade to the Blaze plan; Cloud Firestore's own quotas reset daily around midnight Pacific time. Neither page publishes an inactivity, pause or deletion clock | source: [1] | note: the null is unknown: neither the Firestore quotas page nor the Firebase plans page publishes an inactivity or deletion clock for Spark-plan data; what the free tier does at the limit is a block that lifts at the quota reset or on an upgrade
- egress: 10 GiB a month of outbound data transfer is included in the free quota; beyond it the transfer is billed at the standard Cloud Firestore network rate, and reads are counted as operations against the daily quota | metered: yes | free allowance: 10 GiB per month | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: a Google account
- interface: rest, graphql
- limits:
  - request-rate (binding): 50,000 document reads and 20,000 writes per day [1]
  - per-object-cap: 1 GiB stored; exactly one free database per project [1]
- limits note: a project may hold up to 100 databases, but only one is free, so multiple logical databases is a paid feature
- interface detail: a REST and gRPC API with realtime listeners; SDKs for web, mobile and server; a GraphQL-ish query surface is not offered, the REST and gRPC APIs are
- tooling: the Firebase Admin SDK; the gcloud and firebase CLIs; REST
- composes with: 1 GiB of document state with client SDKs and realtime sync, which no other free tier here gives
- reliability: no suspension, throttle or data-loss event is recorded on the pages read
- notes: The one-database rule is the constraint that a multi-tenant design meets first, not the 1 GiB.
- evidence note: the quotas page was read and states 'exactly one free database per project'.

## Cloudflare D1

- `databases-kv/cloudflare-d1` | qualifies | evidence documented | binding request-rate | category serverless SQLite
- needs card no, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-11-09T14:11:26.568Z (live) | stale on 2026-12-10
- url https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/platform/limits/ | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/cloudflare.md
- price USD 0.75/GB-month beyond 5 GB on Workers Paid | parsed USD 750/TB-mo
- free tier: 10 databases; 500 MB per database; 5 GB per account; 5 million rows read per day; 100,000 rows written per day | unit: mixed | metered on: request-count | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 2,000,000 bytes per row, BLOB or string; 500 MB per database | bytes: 2000000 | source: [2]
- retention: data is kept until it is deleted; at the included 5 GB storage limit D1 blocks inserts, table changes and index creation until data is deleted | source: [1] | note: the null is indefinite: no deletion clock is published; the daily read and write limits reset at 00:00 UTC and refuse queries with an error until then, and the storage limit refuses inserts, table changes and index creation until data is deleted
- egress: no egress charge; rows read and rows written are the metered quantities | metered: no | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: a Cloudflare account
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - request-rate (binding): 100,000 rows written per day on Free [1]
  - request-rate (binding): 5 million rows read per day on Free [1]
  - per-object-cap: 500 MB per database and 5 GB per account; a 2,000,000-byte row ceiling [2]
  - request-rate (binding): 50 queries per Worker invocation on Free; a 30-second maximum query duration [2]
- interface detail: a Worker binding, a REST API and the wrangler CLI
- tooling: wrangler d1; the Cloudflare API; better-sqlite3 style calls inside a Worker
- composes with: per-tenant SQLite in a Worker with a free Postgres as the system of record; 500 MB per database and 10 databases is 5 GB of free relational state
- reliability: at the daily read or write limit the D1 API returns errors; at the storage limit you must delete data before you can insert, alter a table or create an index
- notes: The 100,000 rows written a day is the binding number for any ingest, and it is small: 1.16 rows a second sustained. A full table scan counts every row it scans as a row read, so an unindexed query spends the read budget fast.
- evidence note: the limits and pricing pages were read; nothing was provisioned.
- evidence:
  - [2] 2026-10-22: Free: 10 databases, 500 MB maximum database size, 5 GB per account, Time Travel 7 days, 50 queries per Worker invocation; 2,000,000-byte row maximum; 100,000-byte SQL statement; 30-second query maximum
  - [1] 2026-10-22: Free: 5 million rows read/day, 100,000 rows written/day, 5 GB total storage; 'Free limits reset daily at 00:00 UTC'; at the storage limit you must delete data before inserting
  - [1] 2026-11-09: the Free plan blocks inserts, table changes and index creation at the included 5 GB storage limit until data is deleted | capture: sha256:d0920051e6745a5313cf4100b17c802ce10b10d16eb0cc2a134abee99df95294 | quote: Once you have reached your included storage limit, you will need to delete unused databases or clean up stale data before you can insert new data, create or alter tables or create indexes and triggers.
  - [1] 2026-11-09: the daily read and write limits reset at 00:00 UTC and refuse queries with an error, and the storage limit refuses writes until data is deleted; no deletion of stored data is stated | capture: sha256:d0920051e6745a5313cf4100b17c802ce10b10d16eb0cc2a134abee99df95294 | quote: Free daily usage limits reset at 00:00 UTC. ... When your account hits the daily read and/or write limits, you will not be able to run queries against D1. D1 API will return errors to your client indicating that your daily limits have been exceeded. Once you have reached your included storage limit, you will need to delete unused databases or clean up stale data before you can insert new data, create or alter tables or create indexes and triggers.
  - [2] 2026-11-09: Time Travel is a point-in-time recovery window of 7 days on Free, not a data-retention clock | capture: sha256:bd50f82aed2c4d2387d1eee04fb70f0e269e933f983ebfdd03b97a618ec1facd | quote: | [Time Travel](https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/reference/time-travel/) duration (point-in-time recovery) | 30 days (Workers Paid) / 7 days (Free) |

## Qdrant Cloud

- `databases-kv/qdrant-cloud` | qualifies | evidence documented | binding per-object-cap | category vector database
- needs card no, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-11-09T13:21:21.972Z (live) | stale on 2026-12-10
- url https://qdrant.tech/pricing/ | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/qdrant.md
- free tier: free tier cluster with 1 GB RAM and 4 GB disk, no high availability, one cluster | unit: GB | metered on: stored-bytes | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 4 GB disk per cluster | source: [1]
- retention: free tier clusters are automatically suspended after 1 week of inactivity and deleted after 4 weeks of inactivity if not reactivated; reactivation prevents deletion | days: 28 | source: [2] | note: days is the deletion clock: the cluster is suspended after 1 week of inactivity and deleted at 4 weeks of inactivity; reactivating it before deletion prevents deletion
- egress: not published on the pricing page; recorded as a gap | metered: no | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: email or GitHub signup; no card on Free
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - per-object-cap (binding): 4 GB disk per cluster; 1 GB RAM [1]
  - request-rate: one cluster per account on Free [1]
  - request-rate: no connection limit is published for the free tier; recorded as a gap [1]
- interface detail: a REST API and gRPC; Python, JS and Rust clients
- tooling: the qdrant-client libraries over gRPC or REST
- composes with: the largest free vector storage by disk, and the closest thing to a self-managed index without a host
- reliability: no high availability on the free tier, so the single node is the availability
- notes: 4 GB of disk holds roughly 1.4 million vectors at 768 dimensions and 4 bytes per component, before index overhead. That puts the ~1 million vectors in circulation in the right order. The figure comes from arithmetic, not from a measurement. What happens at 1 GB of RAM is not published. The page offers an upgrade and states no refusal, throttle or deletion. That absence is documented, and it is not headroom.
- evidence note: the pricing FAQ was read; the numbers are in the page's own answers.
- evidence:
  - [1] 2026-10-22: 'The free tier includes 1GB RAM and 4GB disk storage'; the free tier is 'limited to 1GB RAM and 4GB disk without high availability'
  - [2] 2026-11-09: the create-cluster page states free tier clusters are suspended after 1 week of inactivity and deleted after 4 weeks if not reactivated | capture: sha256:bdc2a5ddef5ce5ed983445fe4cd710b182bda104fe3986708fe9f3fcdfb4e32e | quote: If unused, free tier clusters are automatically suspended after 1 week, and deleted after 4 weeks of inactivity if not reactivated. You can upgrade to a standard cluster at any time.
- sources:
  - [1] https://qdrant.tech/pricing/
  - [2] https://qdrant.tech/documentation/cloud/create-cluster/

## TiDB Cloud Starter

- `databases-kv/tidb-cloud-starter` | qualifies | evidence documented | binding request-rate | category distributed SQL, MySQL compatible
- needs card no, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-11-09T13:21:21.973Z (live) | stale on 2026-12-10
- url https://www.pingcap.com/pricing/ | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/pingcap.md
- price USD 0.10 per million RUs beyond the allowance
- free tier: 25 GiB row storage plus 25 GiB columnar storage and 250 million Request Units per month, per organization across up to five instances | unit: GiB | metered on: request-count | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 25 GiB row storage per organization on the allowance; the FAQ states 5 GiB per instance | source: [1] | note: the two first-party pages disagree on whether the allowance is per instance or per org
- retention: once the free quota is reached, the read and write operations on the instance are throttled until a monthly spending limit is set or the usage resets at the start of a new month | source: [2] | note: null is indefinite: no inactivity deletion clock is published; new connections are denied and existing connections are throttled until the quota is increased or the usage resets
- egress: no transfer allowance and no per-GB egress rate is published on the pricing page; recorded as a gap. Traffic is billed through the request-unit and storage meters the page does publish | metered: no | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: email signup for the free allowance; a card only to exceed five instances
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - request-rate (binding): 250 million Request Units per month on the org allowance; the FAQ prints 50 million per instance [1]
  - per-object-cap: 25 GiB row plus 25 GiB columnar per organization; five instances [1]
  - write-gated: a credit card and a spend limit are required to create more than five Starter instances [2]
  - request-rate (binding): 400 concurrent connections per Starter instance, rising to 5,000 with a spending limit; the public-endpoint idle timeout is 340 seconds [3]
- interface detail: the MySQL wire protocol with TLS; a Cloud API and the tiup CLI
- tooling: any MySQL client, the tiup CLI, the Data Migration tool
- composes with: the largest card-free relational allowance found in this class, which is why it is the first row a reader should try
- reliability: no suspension, throttle or data-loss event is recorded on the pages read
- notes: The two pages disagree by a factor of five and the direction matters. 25 GiB per org is the number the pricing page states today; 5 GiB per instance is what the FAQ states. Until one is measured, the conservative reading is 5 GiB per instance and 25 GiB per org across five.
- evidence note: two first-party pages were read and they disagree. The record keeps the conservative per-instance reading and names the disagreement.
- extras:
  - page_disagreement: the docs FAQ's figure is the older per-instance plan and the pricing page's is the current org allowance
- evidence:
  - [1] 2026-10-22: Free monthly allowance: 25 GiB row storage, 25 GiB columnar storage, 250M Request Units, per organization across up to five eligible instances; rates beyond from USD 0.10 per million RUs
  - [2] 2026-10-22: 'Always-free monthly quota for up to five TiDB Cloud Starter instances per organization (5 GiB row data + 5 GiB columnar data + 50 million RUs per TiDB Cloud Starter instance)'; 'you can create a maximum of five TiDB Cloud Starter instances by default. To create more ... you need to add a credit card'
  - [4] 2026-11-09: the FAQ states that reaching the free quota throttles read and write operations until a monthly spending limit is set or usage resets at the start of a new month | capture: sha256:5baf4b75f4fe1b820bf414fcb1f595e9399f813cd13ec3c6307d49803b73b71a | quote: For a free TiDB Cloud Starter instance, once the free quota is reached, the read and write operations on this instance will be throttled until you set a monthly spending limit or the usage is reset upon the start of a new month.
  - [4] 2026-11-09: the FAQ states that reaching the quota denies new connections and throttles existing ones until the quota is increased or usage resets; no deletion is stated | capture: sha256:5baf4b75f4fe1b820bf414fcb1f595e9399f813cd13ec3c6307d49803b73b71a | quote: Once a TiDB Cloud Starter instance reaches its free quota or spending limit, the instance immediately denies any new connection attempts until the quota is increased or the usage is reset at the start of a new month. Existing connections established before reaching the quota will remain active but will experience throttling.

## Turso (Databases and KV)

- `databases-kv/turso` | qualifies | evidence documented | binding retention-clamped | category SQLite at the edge
- needs card no, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-10-22T03:05:00.000Z (live) | stale on 2026-11-22
- url https://turso.tech/pricing | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/turso.md
- price USD 0.75/GB beyond 9 GB on Developer
- free tier: 100 databases; 5 GB storage; 500 million rows read per month; 10 million rows written per month; 3 GB sync | unit: GB | metered on: stored-bytes | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 5 GB across all databases on Free; the plan table gives no per-database cap
- retention: a database is archived after 10 days of inactivity on a free plan, and an archived database must be unarchived before it can be used; a deleted database has no point-in-time restore on Free and the Free column shows 1-day audit logs | days: 10 | source: [2] | note: the archive clock is documented on the CLI and API reference pages, not on the pricing page
- egress: no egress charge and no transfer allowance is published; the metered quantities are rows read and rows written, so a byte of egress is not what is counted | metered: no | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: email signup; GitHub OAuth also offered
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - request-rate: 500 million rows read and 10 million rows written per month [1]
  - per-object-cap: 5 GB total across all databases; 100 databases [1]
  - retention-clamped (binding): an inactive database is archived after 10 days on a free plan [2]
  - request-rate: no connection limit is published on the pricing page or the feature pages; recorded as a gap [1]
- binding note: 10 days of inactivity archives the database on the free plan, so a job that runs less often than that finds the database unavailable. The 5 GB total and the 10-million-row monthly write budget are larger than that clock allows a quarterly job to reach.
- interface detail: libSQL over HTTP and WebSockets; the Turso CLI; a platform API
- tooling: the turso CLI; libSQL client libraries; sqld for a local replica
- composes with: a free SQLite replica per tenant suits multi-tenant read-heavy work that a single free Postgres cannot hold, provided something touches each database at least every 10 days, because the free plan archives an inactive one
- reliability: an inactive database on a free plan is archived after 10 days and must be unarchived before use; the archive is not a deletion and the data survives it
- notes: The 500-database and 9-GB figures in circulation are the Developer plan, not Free. The 5 GB is a total, so 100 databases average 50 MB each. The binding constraint is not either number: it is the 10-day archive, which a quarterly job meets first and which nothing on the pricing page states.
- evidence note: the pricing table was read on 2026-10-22 and its own meta description states 100 databases and 5 GB. The 10-day archive clock is from Turso's CLI reference, read the same day; the pricing page does not carry it, so a reader who checks only the pricing page will not find the constraint that binds first.
- evidence:
  - [1] 2026-10-22: Free column: 100 databases, 5GB storage, 500 Million rows read, 10 Million rows written, 3GB sync, 1 day audit logs; Developer USD 4.99 gives unlimited databases and 9GB
  - [2] 2026-10-22: 'Databases get archived after 10 days of inactivity for users on a free plan'; the unarchive command restores one
  - [3] 2026-10-22: the platform API exposes a group unarchive endpoint, so the archive state is reachable programmatically and not only through the CLI
  - probe:https://api.turso.tech/v1/organizations 2026-10-22: an unauthenticated GET returns 401 with 'token contains an invalid number of segments', proving the platform API exists and is token-authenticated
- sources:
  - [1] https://turso.tech/pricing
  - [2] https://docs.turso.tech/cli/group/unarchive
  - [3] https://docs.turso.tech/api-reference/groups/unarchive

## Upstash Redis (Databases and KV)

- `databases-kv/upstash-redis` | qualifies | evidence measured | binding request-rate | category serverless Redis and KV
- needs card no, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-10-22T03:05:00.000Z (live) | stale on 2026-12-22
- url https://upstash.com/docs/redis/overall/billing | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/upstash.md
- price USD 0.20 per 100K commands; storage USD 0.25/GB-month beyond the first 1 GB | parsed USD 250/TB-mo
- free tier: 250 MB data; 500,000 commands per month; 10 GB bandwidth per month; 10,000 commands per second; one database | unit: mixed | metered on: request-count | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 100 MB per record on Free; 10 MB per request | source: [1]
- retention: a database on a free account persists while the account is active. An anonymous database created with no account is deleted after 3 days unless claimed | days: 3 | source: [2]
- egress: 10 GB bandwidth per month included on Free; pay as you go includes 200 GB then USD 0.03/GB | metered: yes | free allowance: 10 GB per month | price per TB: USD 0.03/GB beyond 200 GB | source: [1]
- identity: anonymous | detail: POST upstash.com/start-redis with an Idempotency-Key provisions a database with no account, no email and no card; the database is deleted after 3 days unless claimed in a browser. A permanent free database needs an email
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - request-rate (binding): 500,000 commands per month on Free, about 16,600 a day [1]
  - per-object-cap: 100 MB per record; 250 MB total data [1]
  - request-rate (binding): 10 GB bandwidth per month [1]
- limits note: adding a payment method moves every database to paid, and 'an account with a payment method cannot have free databases'
- interface detail: a body-style REST API that takes the command as a JSON array; the Redis protocol on the same endpoint; a developer API
- tooling: redis-cli against the TLS endpoint, or any HTTP client against the REST form; @upstash/redis SDKs
- composes with: the cheapest free cache in front of a free Postgres: 100,000 reads a day off the database, if the write path fits 1,000 a day
- reliability: an unclaimed database carries a warning not to store sensitive data because it is not tied to an account; the documented developer API host api.upstash.com did not resolve on 2026-10-22 while the per-database endpoint worked
- notes: The 10,000-commands-per-day figure in circulation is the pre-2025-03 plan. 500,000 a month is 16,600 a day, which is a different shape: a burst is fine and a steady 1/second is not.
- evidence note: a database was provisioned anonymously, PING/SET/GET/DBSIZE were run against it, and the 3-day expiry was read from the response. The free-plan limits are a first-party page.
- evidence:
  - probe:https://upstash.com/start-redis 2026-10-22: POST with Idempotency-Key 5f4fd5c1-7624-43b4-bfc9-94192920d977 returned 200, 3239 bytes, in 7.0 s, with endpoint optimal-spaniel-201484.upstash.io, a bearer token, a console URL and 'Expires: 2026-10-25 (3 days from creation)'
  - probe:https://optimal-spaniel-201484.upstash.io 2026-10-22: body-style REST calls returned PING -> PONG, SET k1 v1 -> OK, GET k1 -> v1, DBSIZE -> 1; each round trip 0.73 to 0.92 s
  - [1] 2026-10-22: Free: 250 MB data, 500K monthly commands, 10 GB monthly bandwidth, 10,000 commands/s, 10 MB request, 100 MB record, 1 database, no credit card
  - probe:https://api.upstash.com/v2/redis/databases 2026-10-22: curl could not resolve api.upstash.com on 2026-10-22, so the documented developer API host is not reachable from this network even though the per-database endpoint is
- sources:
  - [1] https://upstash.com/docs/redis/overall/billing
  - [2] https://upstash.com/start-redis

## Uptrace Cloud

- `databases-kv/uptrace-cloud` | qualifies | evidence documented | binding volume-quota | category managed OpenTelemetry traces, metrics and logs (observability database on ClickHouse) | tier Cloud Free / pay-as-you-go
- needs card no, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-11-19T02:46:18.052Z (live) | stale on 2026-12-20
- url https://uptrace.dev/pricing | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/uptrace.md
- free tier: Uptrace Cloud is free up to 50 GB and 5,000 timeseries per month, then from $0.075/GB with automatic volume discounts; unlimited users, services and hosts. A separate free trial offers 1 TB of storage and 100,000 timeseries with no card required. | unit: GB | metered on: uploaded-bytes | read on: 2026-11-19 | source: [1] | note: The ongoing free allowance is 50 GB per month and 5,000 timeseries; the 1 TB / 100,000-timeseries figure is a signup trial. Metrics are billed per million ingested datapoints from $0.025 per 1M.
- per-object cap: unverified: no single-object cap is published; the free Cloud allowance is 50 GB per month of ingested spans/logs plus 5,000 timeseries, which are volume quotas rather than a per-object cap. | source: [1]
- retention: Uptrace Cloud keeps all data for 4 weeks (28 days) by default; longer cold storage on S3 or HDD is available for up to 100 weeks at $0.01 per GB-month for spans and $0.20 per 1,000 timeseries-month for metrics. | days: 28 | source: [1] | note: 28 days is the default retention; it can be extended via paid cold storage.
- egress: Sending data from AWS or GCP incurs outbound fees; the vendor says OTel Arrow cuts bandwidth 30-70% versus standard OTLP and compresses telemetry 15-30x. Ingestion above the free allowance is charged per GB, not egress from Uptrace. | metered: no | free allowance: 50 GB per month included | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: Cloud signup is a free account with no card required for the trial; billing is handled by Paddle by credit card or bank transfer after signup. A public live demo can be explored without any account.
- interface: rest, cli, browser, chat
- limits:
  - volume-quota (binding): 50 GB free per month and 5,000 timeseries per month on Uptrace Cloud Free; beyond that from $0.075/GB [1]
  - request-rate: Metrics billing starts at $0.025 per 1M ingested datapoints and decreases with volume; minimum supported collection interval is 10 seconds [1]
  - retention-clamped: default retention 4 weeks (28 days); longer storage only via paid cold storage up to 100 weeks [1]
- binding note: The 50 GB/month and 5,000-timeseries free allowance is the first ceiling a free user hits; retention is a fixed 28-day default and per-object caps are not published.
- interface detail: OpenTelemetry OTLP ingest for traces, metrics and logs; Prometheus, Vector, FluentBit and CloudWatch ingest; a built-in MCP server queryable from AI assistants using the existing Uptrace session token; UQL and PromQL-compatible query engines and a web UI.
- tooling: OpenTelemetry SDKs and Collector, Prometheus, Vector, FluentBit, Grafana data-source support; the self-hosted Community Edition that the user installs and runs is the last resort
- composes with: A hosted Uptrace Cloud endpoint takes OTLP telemetry from existing OpenTelemetry instrumentation; self-hosting the AGPL Community Edition on a rented or free machine is the last-resort path when the hosted free allowance is insufficient.
- reliability: Cloud data is stored in Hetzner's Germany datacenters with backups in Finland; 99.9% uptime is listed. Sending from AWS or GCP incurs outbound fees; dropped sampled data costs $0.01 per GB.
- notes: Uptrace Cloud has a genuine ongoing free tier of 50 GB and 5,000 timeseries per month with no card, plus a separate 1 TB / 100k-timeseries signup trial. Paid usage starts at $0.075/GB and data is kept 28 days by default. Self-hosted Community Edition is the last resort, not the offer this record describes.
- evidence note: All stated values come from first-party Uptrace pricing, homepage and signup pages captured on 2026-11-19. The exact signup form fields were not visible in the browser capture and identity is recorded at the level the page shows.
- self hosted: no

- retention: a table and its data persist until the table is deleted or the AWS account is deleted; deleting a table is unrecoverable, and deleting the account removes all of that account's data including tables within 90 days | source: [2] | note: the null is indefinite while the account exists: no inactivity pause or expiry clock is published; data is removed by an explicit DeleteTable (unrecoverable), by deleting the AWS account (all tables within 90 days), or by archiving a table when a customer managed key is lost

- interface detail: an HTTPS JSON API; the AWS CLI and SDKs; PartiQL

- reliability: no suspension, throttle or data-loss event is recorded on the pages read
- notes: 25 RCU is the cap, not 25 GB. Twenty-five strongly-consistent reads a second is a prototype's throughput, and 25 GB of storage behind it will never fill.

Astra is a Serverless Cassandra and vector store, not a general object store, so the lack of a byte cap does not make the credit ceiling irrelevant. The interface is set from the Data API, DevOps API, CQL and CLI documented across the first-party pages.

## Cloudflare Workers KV

- `databases-kv/cloudflare-kv` | qualifies-with-caveat | evidence documented | binding request-rate | category edge key-value store
- needs card no, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-11-09T14:11:26.568Z (live) | stale on 2026-12-10
- url https://developers.cloudflare.com/kv/platform/limits/ | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/cloudflare.md
- free tier: 100,000 reads per day; 1,000 writes per day; 1 GB per account; 1,000 namespaces | unit: requests | metered on: request-count | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 25 MiB per value; 512 bytes per key | source: [1] | note: keys per namespace are unlimited, so the value size is the object cap
- retention: a stored value persists until it expires or is deleted; a write that sets no expiry leaves the value stored indefinitely | source: [2] | note: the null is indefinite: no free-tier deletion clock is published; the daily limits reset at 00:00 UTC, and an operation over a limit fails with an error
- egress: reads are counted, not metered by byte; no egress charge on any plan | metered: no | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: a Cloudflare account
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - request-rate (binding): 1,000 writes per day to different keys [1]
  - request-rate (binding): 1 write per second to the same key [1]
  - per-object-cap: 25 MiB per value; 1 GB per account [1]
- limits note: 100,000 reads per day are unlimited on the paid plan; the minimum cacheTtl is 30 seconds
- interface detail: a REST API and a Worker binding; access through wrangler
- tooling: wrangler kv; the Cloudflare API; a Worker binding in code
- composes with: a read cache in front of a free database: 100,000 reads a day is 100 times the write budget, which is the ratio that makes it a cache and not a store
- reliability: no suspension, throttle or data-loss event is recorded on the pages read
- notes: The asymmetry is the finding: reads are plentiful and writes are not, by two orders of magnitude. Any design that treats KV as the store hits 1,000 writes a day and stops.
- evidence note: the limits page was read; no namespace was created.
- evidence:
  - [1] 2026-10-22: Free column: 100,000 reads/day, 1,000 writes/day to different keys, 1 write/second to the same key, 1,000 namespaces, 1 GB/account, 1 GB/namespace, 512-byte keys, 25 MiB values, 30-second minimum cacheTtl
  - [2] 2026-11-09: a stored value persists until expiry or deletion, and a write with no expiry is stored indefinitely | capture: sha256:79303b52992c22a7b16aebee7b83e7dae1d03ee1fec57f719e2500af4c170c3d | quote: Data cached in Workers KV is accessible from all other Cloudflare locations as well, and persists until expiry or deletion. ... the expirationTtl option is used to set the expiration time for the cache entry (in seconds), otherwise it will be stored indefinitely
  - [3] 2026-11-09: the daily limits reset at 00:00 UTC and an operation over a limit fails with an error | capture: sha256:263f30de3c1e12b828be385ec7915229e9a92072fbe5fc69d11298aab8f27959 | quote: Daily usage limits reset daily at 00:00 UTC. ## Couchbase Capella

- `databases-kv/couchbase-capella` | qualifies-with-caveat | evidence documented | binding retention-clamped | category managed NoSQL document database with key-value, SQL++, search and vector workloads | tier Free
- needs card yes, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-11-19T00:19:24.698Z (live) | stale on 2026-12-20
- url https://www.couchbase.com/pricing | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/couchbase.md
- free tier: One free tier operational cluster per organization: 1 node, 8 GB RAM, 8 to 10 GB data storage depending on cloud, SQL++ and key value, Search (vector, FTS, geo), Mobile App Services, RBAC with scopes and collections, forum support; no credit card required and free for continuous use while active | unit: GB | metered on: stored-bytes | read on: 2026-11-19 | source: [1] | note: The pricing page states 1 node and 8 GB of RAM. Cloud reference pages give the data-storage allowance as 10 GB on AWS and Azure and 8 GB on GCP. The plan is perpetual while the cluster is active, not a trial.
- per-object cap: unverified: the free-tier page does not state a per-document size cap; the Capella Data API platform limit is 100 MB per request and response payload, but that is an interface limit and not a stated per-object cap on the free tier | source: [2] | note: The 100 MB figure is the Data API payload limit and is recorded under limits[] as an interface cap, not as a per-object cap.
- retention: Data and state are preserved while the cluster is active. After more than 72 hours without activity Couchbase turns off the free cluster and linked App Services, preserving data and state; after more than 30 days without activity Couchbase deletes the cluster and linked App Services. Upgrading from the free plan to a paid Support plan also deletes the existing free cluster. | days: 30 | source: [3] | note: days is the inactivity period that triggers deletion. The 72-hour mark only turns the cluster off and preserves data; the 30-day mark deletes it.
- egress: Capella passes through cloud-provider data transfer charges based on GiB and transfer type. Internet egress is commonly .09 credits per GB in North American and European regions; inter-zone or intra-region transfer is commonly .01 credit per GB on AWS and GCP and free on Azure. Data import into Capella and transfer between instances in the same Availability Zone are free. No free egress allowance is published for the free plan. | metered: yes | source: [4]
- identity: email | detail: The sign-up page offers Email Address, GitHub Account or Google Account. The billing docs state no credit balance or credit card is needed for the Free plan.
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - volume-quota: 1 free tier operational cluster per organization; 10 GB data storage on AWS and Azure and 8 GB on GCP; 1 node, 8 GB RAM [5]
  - retention-clamped (binding): cluster turns off after more than 72 hours of inactivity with data preserved, and is deleted after more than 30 days of inactivity [3]
  - request-rate: Data API is limited to 10,000 requests per second per node; payloads restricted to 100 MB [2]
- binding note: The cluster is deleted after 30 days without activity, so a workload with a persistent idle gap fails before the 8 to 10 GB storage or the 10,000 requests per second interface limit is reached.
- interface detail: Couchbase SDKs (Java, Python, Node.js, PHP and others) connect over the couchbases:// TLS protocol; a RESTful Data API exposes document CRUD under /v1/ with passthrough to Query and Search services; a Management API and the Capella web console manage the cluster.
- endpoint: couchbases://<cluster>.dp.cloud.couchbase.com
- tooling: Couchbase SDKs (Java, Python, Node.js, PHP), any HTTP client such as curl or Postman against the Data API, the cbbackupmgr CLI for backup, the Capella web console, and a Management API key for automation
- composes with: A free Capella cluster can hold a document and vector store behind a free Worker or tunnel for a public REST path, with the SDK or Data API as the write interface.
- reliability: The free cluster turns off after 72 hours idle and is deleted after 30 days idle; upgrading to a paid plan deletes the existing free cluster, and the backup and restore, private endpoint, network peering, audit log and on/off schedule features are not available on the free tier.
- notes: The free tier is a real managed Couchbase Server cluster, not a sandbox. Two caveats bind: the cluster is deleted after 30 days idle and upgrading to a paid plan deletes it, so data must be backed out with cbbackupmgr before either. The storage allowance differs by cloud: 10 GB on AWS and Azure, 8 GB on GCP. The per-document cap is not published; the 100 MB figure is the Data API payload limit, not a free-tier object cap. Couchbase Server is also available as self-hosted software, but that offer is the last resort and is not the offer recorded here.

- `databases-kv/mongodb-atlas-m0` | qualifies-with-caveat | evidence documented | binding per-ip-shaping | category document database

- per-object cap: 16 mebibytes per BSON document, which is the MongoDB engine limit and not a tier limit | bytes: 16777216 | source: [2]
- retention: paused automatically after 30 days with zero connections; resumable unless the cluster ran a version Atlas can no longer restore to | days: 30 | source: [1]
- egress: 10 GB in and 10 GB out per rolling seven-day period; exceeding it throttles the cluster and adds a one-second cooldown per connection | metered: yes | free allowance: 10 GB out per 7 days | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: an Atlas account; no card on Free

- limits:
  - per-ip-shaping (binding): 100 operations per second, enforced by throttling with a one-second cooldown [1]
  - per-object-cap: 0.5 GB of data storage; storage size is not configurable on a free cluster [1]
  - request-rate: 10 GB in and 10 GB out per rolling 7-day period [1]
  - retention-clamped: paused after 30 days with zero connections [1]
- limits note: 500 connections maximum; replication factor 3; no sharding, no network peering, and only a subset of regions
- interface detail: the MongoDB wire protocol; a Data API for HTTPS access; the Atlas Administration API and the atlas CLI
- tooling: mongosh, any MongoDB driver, the atlas CLI
- composes with: a free document store that survives inactivity for a month, which is the longest idle clock in this class short of Aiven
- reliability: the page is explicit that Atlas may deactivate idle free clusters under its terms, and recommends exporting a copy before a long pause
- notes: 0.5 GB is a hard wall rather than an overage, and 100 ops/s is a throughput cap that no storage allowance can exceed. The 30-day idle clock is the most forgiving in this class and it is still a clock.
- evidence note: both pages were read on 2026-10-22: the Atlas free-tier limits page for the 0.5 GB, the pause and the throttles, and the server limits page for the 16 mebibyte document cap. The storage figure is 0.5 GB as the page states it. 512 MB is the binary rendering of the same quantity and is not a second figure.
- evidence:
  - [1] 2026-10-22: 'Free clusters: 0.5 GB' for Data Storage; 'Atlas automatically pauses Free clusters after 30 days of inactivity where there are zero connections'; 10 GB in and out per rolling seven-day period; 100 operations per second; 500 connections; 'You can't configure storage size for Free clusters'
  - [2] 2026-10-22: 'The maximum BSON document size is 16 mebibytes', which is an engine limit and not an Atlas tier limit
- sources:
  - [1] https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/free-shared-limitations/
  - [2] https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/limits/

The vector extension was installed and queried, not merely listed as available, so `pgvector on a free Postgres` is a working chain and not an inference.

## Supabase (Databases and KV)

- `databases-kv/supabase` | qualifies-with-caveat | evidence documented | binding retention-clamped | category managed Postgres with auth and storage
- needs card no, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-11-09T12:14:25.959Z (live) | stale on 2026-12-10
- url https://supabase.com/pricing | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/supabase.md
- price parsed USD 25/mo
- free tier: 500 MB database on Shared CPU with 500 MB RAM; 2 active projects; 5 GB egress and 5 GB cached egress; unlimited API requests | unit: mixed | metered on: stored-bytes | read on: 2026-10-22 | source: [1]
- per-object cap: 500 MB per project database | source: [1]
- retention: a Free project is paused after 1 week of low activity, and is restorable for up to 1 year after the pause. A paid project is never paused | source: [2] | note: the pause trigger is activity, not age: a few user requests a day over the previous week keep it awake
- egress: 5 GB egress and 5 GB cached egress per month included. The Free plan publishes no overage price, so the fifth gigabyte is a wall and not a bill | metered: no | free allowance: 5 GB egress, 5 GB cached egress | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: sign-up with an email address and password, or a GitHub, ChatGPT or SSO account
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - retention-clamped (binding): paused after 1 week of low activity; restorable for up to 1 year [2]
  - per-object-cap: 500 MB per database [1]
  - request-rate: 2 active projects per account; paused projects do not count against the limit [3]
  - request-rate: 5 GB egress per month with no published overage path on Free [1]
  - request-rate: connections are set by the compute size and not published as a single number; the free plan runs Nano compute with up to 0.5 GB of RAM, and the pooler queues above the direct limit rather than raising it [4]
- limits note: the shared pooler is IPv4-only on every plan; a direct connection is IPv6-only without the paid IPv4 add-on, so an IPv4-only host must use the pooler
- interface detail: Postgres wire protocol; a PostgREST data API; a Management API and the Supabase CLI
- tooling: psql and any Postgres client; the supabase CLI; PostgREST over HTTP
- composes with: a free Postgres plus free auth plus free object storage in one project, which is the whole reason to pick it over a bare Postgres
- reliability: two warning emails precede an automatic pause, one about a week ahead and one on the pause; restore is a dashboard action, not an API call on the free plan
- notes: Projects on paid plans are not paused for inactivity, so the smallest paid step removes the Free plan's 1-week inactivity pause. That step is Pro, from USD 25 a month: a single database-only project on Micro compute costs USD 25 a month before usage beyond the included quotas, and additional projects add their full compute cost. Pro includes an 8 GB disk per project (then USD 0.125 per GB), 250 GB egress (then USD 0.09 per GB), 250 GB cached egress (then USD 0.03 per GB), 100 GB file storage (then USD 0.0213 per GB) and 100,000 monthly active users (then USD 0.00325 per MAU), plus daily backups stored for 7 days, 7-day log retention and email support. A USD 10 a month compute credit covers one Micro instance, and spend caps are on by default.
- evidence note: the pricing page and the pausing guide were read; nothing was provisioned. The 90-day restore window stated in the 2024-06-24 changelog has since been widened to 1 year.
- extras:
  - monthly_usd: 25

## SurrealDB Cloud

- `databases-kv/surrealdb-cloud` | qualifies-with-caveat | evidence documented | binding request-rate | category multi-model database (document, graph, vector, time-series), serverless and node hosted | tier Earth Free
- needs card yes, phone no, ID no, institution no | verified 2026-11-19T00:19:24.795Z (live) | stale on 2026-12-20
- url https://surrealdb.com/pricing | page https://fshy.ajam.dev/p/surrealdb.md
- free tier: Free $0/mo 3M requests, 10GB storage, no card | unit: mixed | metered on: request-count | read on: 2026-11-19 | source: [1] | note: Earth Free is a monthly allowance of 3M requests, 10 GB storage and 100 database active hours. A separate always-free Cloud single node (1 GB storage, 0.25 vCPU, 1 GB memory) is also listed.
- per-object cap: no per-object cap published on the pricing or Earth limits pages; records and transactions are metered by request units | source: [2]
- retention: Free pauses at a limit and keeps your data; an idle Earth instance scales to zero about 60 seconds after its last query. No automatic deletion of data on the free plan is stated. | source: [1] | note: days null is indefinite: the page states data is kept when the Free allowance is spent.
- egress: | Egressper month | Unlimited | Unlimited | | metered: no | free allowance: unlimited | source: [1]
- identity: email | detail: Create an account with Google, GitHub or email, and sign in. An account needs no payment details. The free instance type carries no charge, so you can deploy before you add a payment method.
- interface: graph, rest, cli
- limits:
  - request-rate (binding): 3M requests per month on Earth Free; 100 clients connected to one instance at once [1]
  - volume-quota: 10 GB storage and 100 database active hours per month on Earth Free [1]
  - write-gated: 100 Earth instances per organisation on Free; deploying is refused when the organisation already has 100 or has spent the month's allowance [2]
- binding note: the 3M-request monthly allowance and the 100-client connection ceiling are reached before the 10 GB storage cap for a typical interactive workload
- interface detail: SurrealQL over WebSocket (wss://<instance-id>.surrealdb.earth/rpc) and HTTP, plus PostgreSQL and MySQL wire protocols; the surreal cloud management CLI and SurrealDB Studio browser UI
- tooling: SurrealDB Studio, surreal cloud CLI, official SDKs, HTTP queries, and psql or mysql clients over TLS
- composes with: the serverless Earth free tier scales to zero and can be reached from a Worker or a server-side app; when steady capacity is needed the paid Cloud single-node plan is the next step
- reliability: Earth is in beta; features, limits and pricing may change before general availability. Earth takes no snapshots and has no backup schedule, and an instance that reaches its Free allowance pauses until the first of the next month.
- notes: The free allowance is shared across all Earth instances in one organisation, so many small databases do not each get 3M requests. Earth cannot coordinate a transaction across instances and has no change feeds, extensions, JavaScript functions or reliable file buckets, so workloads that need those features must use the paid Start or Scale node plans. The always-free Cloud single node (1 GB, 0.25 vCPU) is a separate free offer from Earth Free.
- evidence note: all figures are from first-party pricing and docs pages read; no public read path was probed, so the rung stays documented

- interface detail: a REST API and GraphQL; Python, TypeScript, Java and Go clients
- tooling: the weaviate-client libraries; GraphQL for queries
- composes with: the only free vector tier that caps objects rather than bytes, so it is the right shape for many small records and the wrong shape for a few large ones
- reliability: no suspension, throttle or data-loss event is recorded on the pages read
- notes: One collection is the constraint that decides it. A multi-tenant design that needs a collection per tenant stops at one, and a single collection with 100,000 objects is a small index.

- egress: data transfer is billed separately: same region $0.01/GB, cross region (other regions) $0.02/GB, cross region (APAC) $0.08/GB, Internet $0.10/GB | metered: yes | source: [3]
- identity: email | detail: sign-up creates an account; the free-trial form takes contact details and a free-trial link is sent to the email address. A billing profile with a credit card is needed only to go beyond the free allowance, and the pricing page FAQ states the database-as-a-service is a paid offering
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - volume-quota (binding): 2 vCPU, 16 GiB RAM and 100 GiB storage shared by every cluster in the account [1]
  - retention-clamped: Sandbox cluster: up to 2 vCPU / 4 GB memory / 10 GB storage, up to 15 simultaneous connections, paused after 10 days idle and deleted after 15 days [2]
  - write-gated: larger than free sizes require an Admin to create a billing profile with a payment method [1]
- binding note: The Serverless free allowance is a shared 100 GiB / 2 vCPU / 16 GiB pool, so the storage and compute quota binds before any other stated free limit.
- interface detail: PostgreSQL wire protocol via the YSQL API, plus a Cassandra-style YCQL API; automate with a REST API, CLI or Terraform provider.
- tooling: any PostgreSQL driver or ORM against the YSQL endpoint, CQL drivers against YCQL, the YugabyteDB CLI and Terraform provider; rclone does not apply
- composes with: a free Serverless Postgres database with zero-copy branches behind a worker or tunnel gives a programme-accessible store; the self-hosted open-source YugabyteDB server is a last-resort option and is not the hosted free tier
- reliability: the free allowance runs on a shared pool with resource isolation between tenants; the Sandbox is single-node and is explicitly not for production or performance testing, and it does not support backups.
- notes: The hosted free offer is Serverless Postgres: 2 vCPU, 16 GiB RAM and 100 GiB storage shared across the account, with zero-copy branches. The legacy single-node Sandbox (10 GB, paused after 10 days and deleted after 15) is a different, more restrictive free path and is recorded here as a limit rather than as the headline. The open-source YugabyteDB server is self-hosted software and a last resort, not the hosted free tier. Egress beyond the free allowance is metered in USD per GB.
- evidence note: First-party pages read on 2026-11-19: the Serverless Postgres docs, the Aeon overview, the managed FAQ, the free-trial docs, the billing-profile docs and the pricing page.

The 4GB is the trial deployment size; the docs page gives no per-object cap. The FAQ calls the small Ohio deployment 52ct/hr once the trial ends, and the Developer-deployment blog gives 0.058 USD per hour or 42.2 USD per month for a single-server node.
- per-object cap: unverified: no per-object size cap is stated on the free-tier pages read; the 4GB figure is the deployment size, not a single-object limit | source: [1] | note: ArangoDB is a document store, so the relevant ceiling is the deployment storage; no document-size cap was published on the pages read.

- identity: any-phone | detail: signup asks for an email address required for email verification; if the email is from a public provider such as Hotmail, a mobile phone number is required for SMS verification, and one mobile number cannot be used for multiple accounts. GitHub, Google and Microsoft sign-in are also offered, which avoids the phone step. No card is needed: the FAQ states 'You can sign up on Arango Managed Platform for free without the need to enter a credit card.'
- interface: rest, cli
- limits:
  - retention-clamped (binding): the free deployment is automatically deleted after 14 days, and all data including backups is lost if not converted to a paying account [2]
  - volume-quota: one project and one small deployment of 4GB on the free-to-try tier [1]
  - write-gated: a public email service address triggers a required mobile phone number verified by SMS; one mobile number is bound to one account and cannot be reused [1]
- binding note: the 14-day automatic deletion with no perpetual free lane is what fails first; the 4GB deployment size and the phone gate matter only within that window
- interface detail: the ArangoDB HTTP REST API over TLS, with official drivers for major languages; a web UI (ArangoDB web interface) and a notebook; the FAQ states all ArangoDB drivers are supported as long as TLS is supported
- tooling: any ArangoDB driver over HTTPS (arangojs, python-arango, go-driver and others); the built-in web UI and notebook; rclone does not apply
- composes with: a managed graph, document and key-value store that can sit behind a free frontend or worker for a public endpoint; Foxx services cannot call the internet by default on the managed platform, which limits server-side chaining unless enabled on request
- reliability: the free deployment is deleted at day 14 with all data and backups; single-server and Developer deployments have no high availability and can be restarted at any time; deployments cannot be paused to reduce cost
- notes: ArangoDB Oasis (now Arango Managed Platform) has no perpetual free tier. Its only free route is a 14-day trial with one 4GB deployment, deleted with all data at the end. A public email provider triggers an SMS phone gate bound one-to-one to an account; a GitHub, Google or Microsoft sign-in avoids that gate. The free self-managed Community Edition is software the reader installs and runs, so it is not a hosted offer and is not the answer here. Paid hourly rates begin at 0.058 USD per hour for a single-server Developer deployment and 52ct/hr for a small deployment in Ohio.

The free-tier 4GB and 14-day figures, the identity fields and the deletion clause are quoted from those pages. No probe was run, so the rung stays documented.

Packages are available in the standard repositories of all major Linux distributions and from the MariaDB Foundation download site.
- per-object cap: unverified: no per-object or total size cap stated on the first-party pages read; capacity is set by the machine the user runs the server on | source: [2] | note: This is self-hosted software, so any cap is a property of the user's machine, not of the offer.
- retention: unverified: no retention limit stated on the first-party pages read; data persists on the user's own storage until deleted | source: [2] | note: Retention is determined by the user's own storage and backups, not by the vendor.
- egress: no egress charge or quota applies; the server runs on the user's own machine and network | metered: no | source: [1]
- identity: anonymous | detail: the MariaDB Server download page offers packages and repository setup with no account, card or sign-in; the newsletter email field on that page is an optional subscription, not a download gate
- interface: cli, unknown
- limits:
  - request-rate: max_connections defaults to 151, configurable by the user via an option file or SET GLOBAL [3]
- binding note: This is self-hosted software with no vendor-imposed quota; the only stated configurable limit is max_connections, which the user can raise, so no corpus limit binds the offer itself.
- interface detail: the MySQL/MariaDB wire protocol over TCP with the mariadb command-line client and connectors for C, Java, ODBC, Python and Node.js; the protocol token has no dedicated interface term in the vocabulary
- tooling: the user installs and runs the mariadb-server package or binary on a rented or free machine; connectors exist for C, Java, ODBC, Python and Node.js, and Galera clustering and a Kubernetes operator are available; rclone does not apply
- composes with: a MariaDB Server instance the user installs and runs on a rented or free machine is the self-hosted option of last resort; hosted managed databases such as MariaDB Cloud (MariaDB plc) are separate offers and come first whenever a hosted tier is available
- reliability: LTS releases are maintained for three years; the software is self-operated, so availability and backups depend on the user's own machine.
- notes: The MariaDB Foundation stewards the open source MariaDB Server; it is not a hosted provider. What it offers is software the user installs and runs, so this is the self-hosted option of last resort, recorded behind every hosted database in the topic. MariaDB Cloud is a separate managed offer from MariaDB plc and is not what this record describes. The only quota found on a first-party page is the configurable max_connections default of 151.
